To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

soil water deficit during the fruit development and ripenning phase of processing tomato grown under Mediterranean conditions can be used to increase fruit quality, while maintaining yield, with the use of deficit irrigation strategies.

1) SWD during fruit development and maturation has a significant effect on fruit quality traits, and 2) the response of processing tomato fruit quality traits to SWD depends on the interaction of soil and climate conditions.
fruit firmness, SS and total soluble solids (TSS) increased with SWD, while fruit yield decreased, with the exception of yield and TSS under LD, which were comparable to those of LF.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the possibility of using deficit irrigation to improve fruit quality, and the results suggest that the use of short season irrigation with 50% ET restoration is the most suitable regime to increase SS yield, and to save water in a Mediterranean climate.

a new strategy to reduce water use in processing tomato production, which is based on the possibility of reducing the irrigation amount during the fruit ripening phase without affecting the quality parameters of the crop.
the development of a new approach to the study of the effect of soil and climatic conditions on fruit quality response to SWD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, under deficit irrigation, fruit quality traits were positively correlated, and negatively correlated with fruit yield and size.
the deficit irrigation of processing tomato can be a useful tool to save water and to increase fruit quality, but only if it is carefully planned and implemented.

, in a deficit irrigation program, the best irrigation regime to be applied to processing tomato in the Mediterranean climate is the one which allows a 50% ET restoration up to the beginning of flowering, with a consequent water saving of about 40% with respect to full irrigation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the best strategy for deficit irrigation is to apply water up to 50% ET restoration, but the best timing of deficit irrigation is not clear, and the effect of soil characteristics should also be considered.
the effect of deficit irrigation on tomato fruit quality is site specific.
the effect of SWD on fruit quality is more evident in the first part of fruit development than during ripening.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the fruit firmness and the soluble solids content are the two main traits affected by SWD, and that these traits are strongly influenced by environmental factors, especially by soil and climate characteristics.

the effects of SWD on fruit yield and quality are site-specific, thus the response of processing tomato fruit quality to deficit irrigation is a result of the interaction between soil water availability and environmental conditions.
it is possible to save 47% of water with no yield loss and only a slight reduction in fruit quality, under deficit irrigation, with a long-season irrigation strategy.
